 Why November could bring cooler, active weather changes to central Virginia 
 Unusually early arctic pattern change could push polar air south 
 An unusually early arctic pattern change could push polar air south. (WWBT) By Casey Dorn Published : Oct. 30, 2026 at 7:00 PM EDT | Updated : 23 hours ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google RICHMOND, Va. (WWBT) - Temperatures in October have been above average across central Virginia.
 But an unusually timed change in a large arctic weather pattern could lead to some notable shifts late in November into early December. 
 What We’re Tracking
 Imagine you teleported to the North Pole (hi, Santa!) and stacked three Mount Everests on top of one another. That’s roughly the scale of a massive swirl of air called the polar vortex, found about 90-100,000 feet above the ground.
 This area of low pressure circulates counterclockwise and typically keeps the coldest air bottled up in the Arctic.
 Occasionally, though, energy from lower in the atmosphere pushes upward and essentially throws that entire system into reverse. Temperatures in the stratosphere rise rapidly, and the winds that normally circulate around the pole reverse direction.
 This is called a sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) , and one is likely to occur in the coming week.
 A sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) is likely to occur in the coming week. (WWBT) When this happens, the polar vortex can weaken or split, allowing cold Arctic air to become displaced southward into the mid-latitudes. That includes Virginia, along with much of the United States and parts of Europe.
 What’s the impact?
 Typically, a sudden stratospheric warming can have two major impacts:
 It can lead to outbreaks of cold air, sometimes extending into the eastern United States. 
 It can disrupt the broader polar jet stream, potentially leading to a more active storm pattern. 
 These impacts typically take several weeks to develop after the warming event occurs. That’s because the changes high in the atmosphere need time to work their way downward, eventually influencing weather patterns closer to the surface.
 In this case, we’re looking at late November into early December as a timeframe to watch closely.
 It’s technically possible for this type of event to contribute to snow along the East Coast. But context matters: Richmond has recorded measurable snow in November only once since 2000. That was in 2019, when just 0.9 inches fell.
 So don’t get your hopes too high (or low, depending on your feelings about snow)!
 Part of the uncertainty comes down to exactly where the displaced cold air ends up. It could move into the eastern United States, or it could end up somewhere else, such as western Europe.
 There are a couple of other unusual factors in this setup. For one, we’ve never had a sudden stratospheric warming event occur this early in the season before. We also have a record-strong El Niño to contend with.
 El Niño conditions of this magnitude typically favor above-average precipitation across central Virginia, but also above-average temperatures. That raises an important question: Could El Niño’s influence overpower the colder pattern this Arctic event would typically favor?
 For now, the trend and consistency in the data suggest we should at least expect cooler, closer-to-average temperatures across central Virginia in mid-to-late November. A more significant cold-air outbreak is also possible.
 In addition, this pattern could support coastal nor’easter tracks in late November. Energy from the strong El Niño, combined with the displaced upper-level low pressure, could help keep the storm track closer to the coastline.
 The position of the jet stream and any blocking patterns in the North Atlantic will also be important. Those patterns can influence whether coastal storms track inland, hug the coastline, or move harmlessly out to sea.
 That means regardless of precipitation type, we’re likely looking at a wetter pattern during the second half of the month.
 A Note About November Snow
 While this pattern could support colder temperatures, I’m not particularly enthusiastic about the snow potential just yet.
 Richmond’s November snow history is a good reminder of how uncommon early-season snow can be. The city’s top five November snow totals on record are:
 YEAR TOTAL SNOW (INCHES) 
 1953 7.3 
 1987 4.5 
 1938 4.4 
 1929 3.8 
 1912 2.0 
 Interestingly, both 1953 and 1987 featured El Niño conditions in the Pacific Ocean, although those were weak-to-moderate events. Those are more favorable for cold air to be aligned with good moisture across the East Coast.
 There also isn’t a strong correlation between El Niño events and Richmond’s wettest Novembers on record.
 The bottom line: 
 There are some interesting signals in the atmosphere worth watching, but there is still plenty of uncertainty. Cooler temperatures and an active storm pattern are possibilities. Snow is on the table, but it’s far too early to get excited about that possibility.
